title: Editorial: A tumultuous two decades in Cape wine
summary:

The post Editorial: A tumultuous two decades in Cape wine appeared first on winemag.
content:
South Africa’s national wine-grape vineyard peaked at just over 102,000 hectares in 2006, following the red-wine planting boom that began after political transformation in the 1990s. It has been in decline ever since.

Look back at the wines, winemakers and businesses that commanded attention in 2006 and it becomes clear that continuity is hard to achieve: some brands have endured, but many have changed hands, lost ground or disappeared. The Cape wine industry is in a constant state of flux, and succession remains one of its more difficult challenges.

The Platter’s 2006 edition, published towards the end of 2005, awarded just 10 Five Star ratings. Wine of the Year was Glen Carlou Syrah 2004, made by David Finlayson. His father, Walter, founded the Paarl property in 1985; Swiss businessman and art collector Donald Hess bought out the family in 2003. Hess then sold Glen Carlou to the South African Pactolus Consortium in December 2016. David had left in 2009 to establish his own brand, Edgebaston. The property and its winemaker had taken different paths.

Consulting old copies of Wine magazine shows, however, that some things do endure. Boplaas dominated the Port category then, as it does now, while Raats was already setting the pace for Cabernet Franc. Spier, too, continues to make its presence felt in Chenin Blanc: its Private Collection 2004 won the TOPS at SPAR Chenin Blanc Challenge then, while its 21 Gables 2024 earned Double Gold at this year’s Veritas. The Nel family at Boplaas and Bruwer Raats at Raats Family Wines retain control of their respective businesses. Spier, orders of magnitude larger, demonstrates that family ownership and active custodianship can sustain a distinctive identity and remain competitive at scale.

Michel Rolland, the influential French consultant winemaker who died earlier this year aged 78, had advised Rupert & Rothschild since 1999 and was also a shareholder in Remhoogte. His involvement reflected the international influences shaping Cape wine, including a shift towards riper, more opulent reds that appealed to critics such as Robert Parker. Foreign investment has hardly been a passing phase: it continues to bring capital, expertise and market access to South African wine, and the industry would arguably be in a considerably more precarious position without it. The challenge is to harness that investment while retaining the character and credibility of Cape wine.

Laibach 2003 was named the best Merlot in a category tasting convened by Wine magazine. Kanonkop acquired the property around the turn of 2021–22 and subsequently absorbed it into the larger operation. Former Laibach winemaker François van Zyl became Kanonkop head winemaker in late 2024, seemingly the ideal successor to the long-serving Abrie Beeslaar, before leaving unexpectedly in June 2026. His departure underlined the difficulty of succession: finding the right person is one thing; keeping them is another.

Pinot Noir was a hotly contested, if small, category: 27 wines featured in the tasting, with only two earning Four Stars, Sumaridge 2004 and Hamilton Russell Vineyards 2004. Hamilton Russell remains a significant producer, if not necessarily the unchallenged leader of the category. Sumaridge was acquired by Belgian couple Céline Haspeslagh and Frederik Herten in 2021 and relaunched as Hasher Family Wines. Sumaridge never really established a strong brand identity, and its successor has yet to do so either.

Vergelegen was the most successful producer at the fifth annual Trophy Wine Show, with André van Rensburg at the height of his powers. He left the Somerset West property in 2022 after 25 harvests, an unusually long tenure in an industry where winemakers frequently move between properties. Saxenburg Private Collection Shiraz 2003, meanwhile, was named the best wine overall in the Shiraz Challenge, made by the veteran Nico van der Merwe, who left in 2017 to concentrate on his own label. Their departures illustrate how difficult it can be to sustain a successful winemaking identity beyond the person most closely associated with it.

Vin de Constance 2001 from Klein Constantia took top honours in the natural sweet wine category. The Jooste family sold the property in 2011 to Czech-American businessman Zdeněk Bakala and Englishman Charles Harman. The Vin de Constance name and reputation have endured under new ownership, but inheritance alone is no guarantee of continuity. The brand has been expertly managed, demonstrating that while consumer loyalty may be inherited, sustaining it requires skill and commitment.

Chris Mullineux and his then-fiancée Andrea (née Kozlowski) were beginning to attract attention after taking charge at Tulbagh Mountain Vineyards in November 2002. They would go on to establish Mullineux Wines in the Swartland, becoming two of the defining figures of a new generation.

Rustenberg John X Merriman 2003, made by Adi Badenhorst, was the leading Cape Bordeaux-style red blend in the category tasting, with a Four-and-a-Half-Star rating. Badenhorst would later leave the Stellenbosch property in 2007, also to establish himself in the Swartland. Rustenberg remains commercially successful, but it is arguable that it has not enjoyed the same level of critical attention since.

The winner of the Amorim Cork Cap Classique Challenge, then still convened by Wine magazine, was Desiderius Pongrácz 2001, made by Wilhelm Pienaar. Pienaar moved to Hermanuspietersfontein to focus mainly on Sauvignon Blanc in 2013, following Bartho Eksteen’s departure.

White blends, whether Bordeaux-inspired or built around Chenin Blanc in a more distinctly Cape idiom, were just beginning to attract serious attention. Two leading examples identified by the Wine magazine panel were Palladius 2004, only the third vintage of Eben Sadie’s ambitious white blend, and Cape Point Vineyards Isliedh 2005. Duncan Savage joined Cape Point in 2002 and remained there until 2016, before concentrating on Savage Wines. Today, Palladius is an established reference point for Swartland white blends, while Isliedh remains part of the Cape Point story, despite uncertainty over ownership.

The year ended with the announcement of Gottfried Mocke as Diners Club Winemaker of the Year for Chamonix Reserve 2005. Mocke left the Franschhoek property in 2015 to join Boekenhoutskloof.

The upshot is that while some brands and properties have proved remarkably durable, others have been reshaped by new owners, new winemakers or changing commercial realities.

The industry’s current challenges are considerable: a shrinking vineyard area, pressure on margins, changing patterns of consumption and the need to make South African wine relevant to a new generation of drinkers. Yet the past 20 years suggest that the next chapter will not unfold as anyone expects. The people who seem indispensable today may be gone tomorrow; properties that appear securely established may change hands, while unheralded producers may become the names everyone wants to talk about.

Wine is an agricultural product, a commercial undertaking and a cultural expression, all at once. It is shaped by forces no single winemaker or owner can fully control. Continuity matters, but so does renewal. The challenge is not to prevent change, but to manage succession well enough to preserve the best of what has been built. The past two decades offer no reliable template for what comes next.

title: Tim James: Who really wins at wine auctions?
summary:
The Strauss & Co wine auctions began in 2019, in good time to benefit, as is clear in retrospect, from the pandemic that was soon to hit us. The stated aim was “elevate South African wines to the same degree of collectability as the visual and decorative arts”. To many ordinary wine lovers, however, I […]

The post Tim James: Who really wins at wine auctions? appeared first on winemag.
content:
The Strauss & Co wine auctions began in 2019, in good time to benefit, as is clear in retrospect, from the pandemic that was soon to hit us. The stated aim was “elevate South African wines to the same degree of collectability as the visual and decorative arts”. To many ordinary wine lovers, however, I suggested at the time, the idea of wine becoming “an exciting new asset class” for the rich was not entirely welcome.

It’s been interesting since then to watch the progress in building a vibrant secondary market for South African wine. Talking of that first auction at the time, in a piece on “The rise of wine speculation in South Africa’, I expressed doubts about whether there was a large enough supply of genuinely top-end wine to allow for a sustainable system of auctions; also about whether the ageability of Cape wines was sufficient to justify speculation.

It’s probably still early days (remember what Zhou Enlai didn’t actually say about it still being too early to judge whether the French Revolution had been successful or not?), but the evidence has been equivocal. On the one hand, Strauss has successfully held a great many wine auctions – of both local and foreign wines – since then, many of them with all the lots on offer sold; and other auction houses have also found it worthwhile to dabble. (One such was Aspire, working with Rueda Wine Company; their last wine auction, in June, went pretty badly and in fact the auction house seems to have ceased business.) And there are other places that give evidence of a developing secondary market, like the brokerage section of Brice & Burnett.

On the other hand, as Michael Fridjhon pointed out in a little debate with Strauss’s Roland Peens on this website, offered volumes have been very small, which has helped sustainability. At least as importantly, the number of Cape wines that have been truly successful on the auction has been tiny, most notably from Kanonkop and Sadie, Meerlust, Klein Constantia (for Vin de Constance), Vilafonté, Alheit, and Mullineux, with Porseleinberg also very much there – but even not all of those overwhelmingly so.

I did some work on the Strauss records a year ago and demonstrated a degree of recent decline in prices and in sales. I pointed out that it’s not at all uncommon for wines to sell below the estimates offered by the auctioneer. More importantly, I argued, looking at the numbers, that although a few wines sold consistently at high prices, making a decent return for the sellers, that was certainly not true even for many pretty famous wines. One of many examples I offered was Le Riche Cab Reserve 2015 selling for little more than the current release, not even taking into account the seller’s commission (15%) to the auctioneer. That sort of thing is not untypical.

I’ve done some similar sums for recent auctions, and the picture is repeated: a great many sellers are not making much, or even any, profit on their original purchase price, especially taking inflation and costs of storage into account. This is often great for buyers, of course, and the auctioneer still takes two bites of the money . Just a few examples of the arithmetic here. In June, Alheit Cartology 2019 sold, below estimate, for R781 per bottle (including buyer’s premium-and-VAT). That would mean the seller received about R538 (after deducting seller’s commission-and-VAT on the hammer price; my thanks to Michael Fridjhon for working out the arithmetical formula that is quite beyond my capabilities). And R538 is very little more than the current retail price of the 2025.

Even more depressingly for the seller, David & Nadia Chenin Blanc 2019 sold, below estimate, for R547 per bottle in the same auction. The current retail price for 2025 is about R505. The Strauss seller would have received R377. Even Sadie Palladius 2019 went for just R1954 per bottle, and a case of 2017 went unsold. To return to my earlier example of Le Riche Reserve: the 2015 sold for a little more than it did last year, at R1563 per bottle (in a six-bottle case), meaning the seller got R1078 per bottle and would have to pay more to replace it with the current release.

The sellers were not exactly rejoicing, I imagine, in what was intended to be the nascent triumph of a secondary market for fine South African wine. As I say, a few wines are selling well in very small volumes, and buyers are getting some great bargains in fine South African wine. But sellers doing well? Not so much. A sustainable secondary market at this rate? Hmmm….

There’s a different but related aspect of the recent auctions that is intriguing me, and arguably gives further support to my early concerns about the sustainability of these auctions as originally conceived.

If the Strauss wine auctions were founded with a lot of trumpeting about “elevating” South African wines, and building a secondary market for them, well, that’s not at all how things are looking now. Let’s leave aside the Winemakers Guild auction conducted by Strauss, which is of course not about a secondary market. For Strauss auctions generally, non-South African wines now predominate in number as well as value (I strongly suspect that they have for some years been the biggest money-makers for the auction house). Possible sellers of local wines have lost some of their initial enthusiasm – and, dare I say, naivety? – or no longer have much in the way of excess stocks.

The current auction offers wines only “from Italy, Spain, Germany, the Rhône Valley and more”. September was “South African Wine Legends & Classified Bordeaux”; August: “Burgundy and Champagne”; July: “Italy, Spain and Portugal Fine Wine”; May: Bouchard Père burgundies;  etc. June’s was in fact the only auction this entire year devoted entirely, to local wines and included everything from table wines through to brandy. The other 2026 auctions were entirely of often rather grand European wines, going for grand prices, or having South African wines as the minority component of the sale. I must say, in brackets as it were, that I have been somewhat stupefied to see the extent and depth and value of foreign wine holdings emerging from local cellars.

This current preponderance might just be coincidence, though I see no reason why it should be, and auctions in 2027 will tell a different tale. But I strongly suspect that the central intention to “elevate” South African wines and to develop the secondary market has been quietly subordinated by Strauss, and their wine auctions are just another place dealing in luxury goods for the rich – who clearly have a great deal of money and are more interested in spending it on the big wine names of Europe.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

content:
Category Reports, sponsored by Prescient Fund Services, are being released across four seasonal series: Autumn, Winter, Spring and Summer. The first three are now complete, with Summer still to come.

The following reports are now open for entry (click the report name for details):

Cap Classique

Sauvignon Blanc and Sauv-Sem blends

Rosé

The wines will be tasted by editor Christian Eedes, Ndaba Dube, Director of Operations, President Hotel, Cape Town, and wine writer Malu Lambert.

Why enter?

  • Your wine is judged blind, without producer or brand influencing the result.
  • Every entry receives a Winemag 100-point score.
  • The Top 10 receive individual tasting notes.
  • Inclusion in a buyer’s guide, ranking wines by quality relative to price.
  • Your wine is assessed alongside other leading examples in its category.
  • Best Overall recognition goes to the highest-performing wine in the tasting.

Entry fee: R1,495 per wine, including VAT.

Prize

The producer of the best wine overall in each of the respective categories wins shipping services worth R10 000 from Aspiring Couriers.

The post Prescient Fund Services Rosé Report 2026: Rules and entry form appeared first on winemag.
content:
Rules

  • Only still wines are eligible.
  • All types of rosé are eligible, “rosé” defined as a wine incorporating some colour but not enough to qualify it as a red wine. Production methods allowed include: 1) direct pressing of red wine grapes; 2) short maceration of red wine grapes; 3) saignée – bleeding off of juice; 3) blending of juice from red and white wine grapes; and 4) white wine aged in vessels previously used to mature red wine. Wines labelled as “Blanc de Noir” are automatically allowed.
  • Wines must be certified as South African.
  • Wines entered must be current release or soon to be released (minimum stock requirement: 100 x 6 bottles). Producers may enter as many different wines as they see fit.
  • Entries close Wednesday 11 November. An entry sample takes the form of two bottles. There are two submission methods – please indicate the number corresponding to your chosen option on the entry form:
  1. collection by Aspiring Couriers (login and create a waybill here)
  2. delivery to Aspiring Couriers, 37 Muscat Road, Saxenburg Park 1, Blackheath, Cape Town
  3.  
  • The deadline for the submission of samples is 17h00 on Thursday, 12 November. LATE SUBMISSIONS WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED.
  • In the event a wine achieves Top 10 status, 18 bottles must be set aside at no charge, these to be served at promotional events.

To enter, kindly ensure you (or the company you represent) are a subscriber to Winemag.co.za. If you’re not yet subscribed, click here to sign up.

An entry fee of R1,495 including VAT per wine applies and you will be directed to our online shop to make payment after you have completed the entry form below. Please note that if you want to enter multiple wines, each will require a separate form although payment can be made all at once.

title: Cape Winemakers Guild Auction 2026 sales figures
summary:
The 42nd Cape Winemakers Guild Auction, held on 2 and 3 October, generated R18.22m in sales, up 5.9% on 2025. There were 2,220 cases sold, versus 1,912 last year, an increase of 16%. In other words, more wine shifted and more money raised, but the average price per bottle fell from R1,501 to R1,368. Hosted […]

The post Cape Winemakers Guild Auction 2026 sales figures appeared first on winemag.
content:
The 42nd Cape Winemakers Guild Auction, held on 2 and 3 October, generated R18.22m in sales, up 5.9% on 2025. There were 2,220 cases sold, versus 1,912 last year, an increase of 16%. In other words, more wine shifted and more money raised, but the average price per bottle fell from R1,501 to R1,368.

Hosted by Strauss & Co, the hybrid event (bids accepted in person, online and by telephone) drew 263 registered bidders from 16 countries. 58 wines were offered: 34 reds (1,364 cases), 22 whites (780 cases) and two Cap Classiques (76 cases).

For the first time in the Guild’s 42-year history, white wines, including Cap Classique, achieved a higher average price than reds: R1,416 per bottle versus R1,340, excluding VAT. Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay accounted for 65% of the white wines offered.

The five producers achieving the highest six-bottle-equivalent hammer prices were:

  1. Mullineux The Gris Old Vine Sémillon 2025 – R27,500
  2. Rall Wines Noa Syrah 2024 – R19,000
  3. Leeu Passant Hillside Cabernet Franc 2023 – R17,500
  4. Solo Wines by Carl Schultz CWG Auction Merlot 2023 – R15,000
  5. Van Loggerenberg Wines CWG Auction Syrah 2025 – R13,000

The 96 successful bidders included two private clients among the top 10 buyers, alongside Grootbos, Singita and UK merchant Bordeaux Index.

South African bidders accounted for 78% of sales, the balance hailing from 10 other countries: the UK, Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Hong Kong, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Guernsey and Australia; UK bidders accounted for 7% of the total.

Trade represented just under 30% of bidders but accounted for 44% of the total value purchased.

Separately, the Cape Winemakers Guild Protégé Auction raised R655,900 through donated wines and wine-related experiences. The money supports the Guild’s Protégé Programme, which provides placements and training for emerging South African winemakers.
